title: Hardware, Runtime, and Capacity Planning
summary: Select a compatible runtime and size compute, accelerator memory, host memory, storage, and concurrency from measurements of the exact serving build.
objectives: Build a compatibility matrix across artifact format, model architecture, runtime, accelerator, drivers, operating system, and deployment target.
Estimate static model memory, dynamic cache and workspace memory, host memory, storage, bandwidth, and startup needs without treating an estimate as a benchmark.
Measure latency, throughput, concurrency, saturation, errors, and resource headroom with representative request distributions.
Produce a capacity decision with resource limits, admission control, overload behavior, cost assumptions, and re-benchmark triggers.

sections.title: Prove compatibility across the complete stack
paragraphs: Record the model architecture, artifact and tensor formats, precision or quantization, tokenizer, template, maximum tested context, runtime and version, execution backend, operating system, CPU architecture, accelerator model, accelerator count, driver, compute library, container base, and required extensions. Verify support from current runtime and hardware documentation and then load the exact artifact in quarantine.

A runtime may support an architecture but not a specific conversion, quantization, kernel, device, platform, or feature combination. Automatic fallback can silently move work to a slower backend or change behavior. Make fallback visible, measured, and either accepted or rejected.

Use one of four evidence labels for every cell. Documented means a cited source describes the exact value or support claim. Measured means the exact build produced retained evidence. Inferred means a calculation or analogy suggests the value but has not established it. Unknown means the evidence is absent. An architecture name or model-family name never upgrades an exact runtime, quantization, kernel, or device combination from unknown to compatible.

Worked synthetic matrix for build caplab-1: model architecture = exercise transformer [documented by fixture specification]; artifact revision and digest = synthetic-capacity-artifact@sha256:fixture-only [documented, not a real model]; tensor format = synthetic packed tensors [documented]; precision or quantization = 4 bits per parameter plus 0.5 GiB metadata [documented]; tokenizer = fixture-tokenizer-v1 [documented]; prompt template = fixture-chat-v1 [documented]; maximum context = 4,000 input-plus-output tokens in the accepted slice [measured only by deterministic fixture arithmetic, not by a model]; runtime = Node.js 22 native ESM calculator [measured by the offline test when run]; execution backend = arithmetic fixture, no inference backend [documented]; operating system = learner host [unknown until recorded]; CPU architecture = learner host [unknown until recorded]; accelerator model and count = proposed single 24 GiB-class device [inferred sizing target, exact model unknown]; driver and compute library = not used by the fixture and unknown for a real deployment [unknown]; container base = none in the exercise [documented]; extensions = none [documented]. Because accelerator, driver, model artifact, and inference runtime compatibility are unknown, this matrix cannot approve a real deployment.

Transfer record for broader self-hosted ecosystems: Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Microsoft Phi, and NVIDIA software each have distinct model artifacts, licenses, templates, runtime paths, and hardware constraints. Their official repositories in the source list are discovery evidence, not proof that one common runtime or API supports every family. For each candidate, copy the full matrix and leave exact artifact/runtime/backend/driver/accelerator compatibility UNKNOWN until documentation and a quarantine load of that exact combination establish it. NVIDIA can name a hardware or software ecosystem, while Meta, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, and Phi can name model families; none of those names alone specifies an interchangeable API or a verified serving build.

Causal checkpoint: if a learner marks the proposed accelerator combination measured merely because the arithmetic fits under 24 GiB, return to the evidence labels. Capacity arithmetic addresses size, while compatibility requires the exact artifact to load and execute on the exact stack. The correction is to retain UNKNOWN compatibility and schedule a quarantined integration test.
sections.callout: Family-level support is not exact-stack compatibility. Unknown combinations are excluded from the final realistic deployment decision.

sections.title: Estimate memory and storage before measuring
paragraphs: Begin with the exact artifact sizes and a rough weight-memory estimate from parameter count and bits per parameter, then add quantization metadata, embeddings, runtime workspace, graph or kernel caches, temporary buffers, loaded replicas, and safety headroom. Dynamic memory also depends on concurrent sequences, context and output lengths, cache representation, batching, and runtime behavior.

Include host memory for the runtime, tokenizer, request queues, observability, page cache, staging, and failure handling. Include local and remote storage for immutable artifacts, container layers, caches, logs, evaluation data, backups, and rollback bundles. Treat every calculation as a hypothesis to validate on the intended build.

Keep decimal GB and binary GiB explicit. One GB is 1,000,000,000 bytes and one GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes. Do not add GB and GiB without conversion. Accelerator memory, host memory, and storage are separate ledgers. A free accelerator GiB does not compensate for exhausted host memory or storage.

Synthetic assumptions fixed before results: 16 billion parameters at 4 bits each gives 16,000,000,000 × 4 ÷ 8 = 8,000,000,000 bytes, or 8 GB and approximately 7.451 GiB. The exercise rounds the loaded static allocation upward to 10 GiB to include metadata and runtime allocations. Add 2 GiB workspace and 2 GiB accelerator safety headroom. The synthetic dynamic cache rate is 0.5 GiB per concurrent request per 1,000 maximum tokens. This rate is a fixture assumption, not a statement about any real model or runtime.

Three reproducible scenarios use accelerator total GiB = 10 static + 2 workspace + 2 safety + concurrency × maximum tokens ÷ 1,000 × 0.5. Scenario A, 2 concurrent requests at 2,000 tokens: dynamic = 2 × 2 × 0.5 = 2 GiB and total = 16 GiB. Scenario B, 4 concurrent requests at 4,000 tokens: dynamic = 4 × 4 × 0.5 = 8 GiB and total = 22 GiB. Scenario C, 5 concurrent requests at 4,000 tokens: dynamic = 5 × 4 × 0.5 = 10 GiB and total = 24 GiB. Against the predeclared 23 GiB admission ceiling, A and B fit while C must be rejected. The deliberate lab defect incorrectly reports 14 GiB for all three by omitting the dynamic term.

The independent host ledger is 6 GiB runtime and tokenizer + 2 GiB queues + 1 GiB observability + 2 GiB page cache + 2 GiB staging + 2 GiB failure handling + 3 GiB recovery headroom = 18 GiB against a 24 GiB host limit. The storage ledger is 12 GiB artifacts + 4 GiB container layers + 6 GiB caches + 5 GiB logs + 3 GiB evaluation data + 12 GiB backup + 12 GiB rollback copy = 54 GiB against an 80 GiB limit. Rollback is a separate retained copy, not an assumption that the active artifact can be overwritten.

The startup transfer fixture uses decimal units: 12 GB ÷ 1.5 GB/s = 8 seconds under an idealized constant-bandwidth assumption. This excludes authentication, latency, decompression, checksum verification, filesystem contention, and runtime initialization, so it is an estimate rather than a measured startup time. The cost fixture is USD 2.40 per replica-hour × 24 hours = USD 57.60 per replica-day. It excludes tax, storage, network, support, idle reserve, and regional variation and is not a cloud quote.

Causal checkpoint: if Scenario C is admitted, inspect whether cache is multiplied by both maximum tokens and concurrent requests. Deny-all is also incorrect because Scenario B is genuinely under the 23 GiB ceiling. A valid repair changes only the missing dynamic cache term and preserves validation, host, storage, startup, and cost calculations.
sections.callout: A model that fits at startup may still fail under long contexts, concurrency, batching, or recovery.

sections.title: Measure a representative request distribution
paragraphs: Version a load profile containing warm and cold starts, input and output token distributions, modalities, concurrency steps, bursts, cancellations, timeouts, malformed requests, maximum allowed context, and recovery after pressure. Measure time to ready, time to first output, inter-output latency where applicable, end-to-end latency percentiles, throughput, queue time, error and rejection rates, accelerator and host memory, compute utilization, storage and network behavior, power where relevant, and restart time.

Hold the artifact, runtime, configuration, hardware, prompt template, and cases constant when comparing builds. Published benchmark results can help frame methods and candidate hardware, but they do not replace measurements of the exact workload, software stack, quality target, and service policy.

Thresholds are fixed before inspecting the synthetic traces. For the supported steady and burst slices: nearest-rank p95 end-to-end latency must be at most 800 ms, nearest-rank p95 queue time at most 100 ms, successful throughput at least 8 requests/s, internal error rate at most 1 percent, accelerator allocation at most 23 GiB, and host allocation at most 24 GiB. The maximum-context boundary has a separate throughput floor of 4 requests/s. Controlled admission rejection during overload is expected, but admitted requests must have zero internal errors in this small fixture. Restart time to ready must be at most 60 seconds, and the recovery case must pass the steady thresholds.

Arithmetic contract: sort all observations ascending and select nearest-rank p95 at rank ceiling(0.95 × n), using one-based ranks. Successful throughput is completed requests divided by duration seconds. Internal error rate is internal errors divided by admitted requests; a zero admitted denominator is invalid rather than reported as zero. Rejection rate is rejected requests divided by offered requests. Cancellations requested by clients are recorded separately from internal errors.

Exact synthetic trace load-profile-v1: warmup offers 2 requests at concurrency 1 after a cold start, with latencies [1800,1200] ms, queue times [0,0] ms, 2 completions, 0 errors, 0 rejections, and 45 seconds to ready; warmup is excluded from steady latency SLOs. Steady state offers 10 requests over 1 second at concurrency 4 with sorted latencies [420,440,460,470,490,510,540,580,620,700] ms, sorted queue times [5,8,10,12,15,18,20,25,30,40] ms, 10 completions, 0 errors, accelerator 22 GiB, and host 18 GiB. Its p95 ranks are both 10, so p95 latency is 700 ms, p95 queue is 40 ms, throughput is 10 requests/s, and error rate is 0 percent: pass.

Burst offers 10 requests over 1 second at concurrency 4 with latencies [500,520,540,560,590,610,650,700,740,780] ms and queue times [10,15,20,25,30,40,50,60,75,90] ms, 10 completions, 0 errors, accelerator 22 GiB, and host 18 GiB. P95 latency is 780 ms, p95 queue is 90 ms, and throughput is 10 requests/s: pass. Maximum context offers 5 requests over 1 second at concurrency 4 and 4,000 tokens, with latencies [620,680,720,760,790] ms, queue times [20,30,40,60,80] ms, 5 completions, 0 errors, and 22 GiB accelerator allocation. P95 latency is 790 ms and throughput is 5 requests/s: pass its declared boundary thresholds.

Overload offers 10 requests at concurrency 5 and 4,000 tokens. Correct pre-execution arithmetic requires 24 GiB, so all 10 are rejected before model execution, no request is admitted, and no internal error rate is computed because its denominator would be zero. The rejection rate is 10 ÷ 10 = 100 percent and the reason is capacity_limit. Cancellation offers 5 at concurrency 4, records 1 client cancellation, 4 completions, 0 internal errors, and 0 capacity rejections. Restart records 45 seconds to ready, below the 60-second limit. Recovery then offers 10 requests over 1 second at concurrency 4 with latency p95 720 ms, queue p95 45 ms, 10 completions, 0 errors, accelerator 22 GiB, and host 18 GiB: pass.

These are deterministic fixture traces, not executions of Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi, NVIDIA software, an accelerator, Docker, Kubernetes, or a cloud API. A real integration must replace fixture values with timestamped measurements from the exact artifact, runtime, backend, driver, accelerator, host, container, and request corpus. No model download, API key, deployment approval, or cloud charge is part of this lesson.

Causal checkpoint: if the learner reports overload as a 0 percent internal error rate, point to the zero admitted denominator. The correct result is not applicable for that rate, alongside a 100 percent controlled rejection rate. If warmup latency is silently mixed into steady state, the learner has changed the declared population and must recompute or restore the versioned profile.
sections.callout: Fixture simulation teaches the measurement contract. It does not certify real-model latency, throughput, quality, power, compatibility, or recovery.

sections.title: Find saturation and design overload behavior
paragraphs: Increase concurrency and request size gradually until latency, queueing, memory, errors, power, or quality crosses a declared boundary. Record the first limiting resource and the failure mode. Repeat after restarts and with neighboring workloads if resources are shared.

Set container or scheduler requests and limits from evidence, leaving headroom for the host and recovery. Docker documents that containers have no resource constraints by default, and memory pressure can trigger out-of-memory termination. Admission control, bounded queues, maximum context and output limits, rate or concurrency limits, timeouts, load shedding, and clear retry behavior are part of capacity—not afterthoughts.

Synthetic saturation sweep: concurrency 2 at 2,000 tokens requires 16 GiB and is admitted; concurrency 4 at 4,000 tokens requires 22 GiB and is admitted; concurrency 5 at 4,000 tokens requires 24 GiB and crosses the fixed 23 GiB ceiling. The first fixture boundary is therefore accelerator admission memory, specifically dynamic per-concurrent-request cache. This is arithmetic evidence only, not an observed out-of-memory event or hardware benchmark.

The policy admits at most 4 concurrent requests when each may reach 4,000 tokens under these fixture assumptions. It validates token and unit fields, uses a bounded queue outside the calculator, rejects over-limit work before allocation with reason capacity_limit, does not retry nontransient capacity rejections automatically, and preserves 1 GiB between the 23 GiB admission ceiling and a nominal 24 GiB device class. Real queue length, timeout, output-token cap, cancellation cleanup, and retry-after values remain UNKNOWN until exact-build tests establish them.

Docker resource limits and Kubernetes requests and limits are deployment controls, not proofs of application fit. Docker documents that containers have no resource constraints by default, that hard memory limits and softer reservations differ, and that swap can impose performance costs. Kubernetes distinguishes scheduling requests from enforced limits. Preserve the 3 GiB host recovery headroom and test restart behavior rather than assigning every host byte to the serving process.

Causal checkpoint: if the learner fixes overload by always returning admit false, run the base scenario. It must remain admitted at 22 GiB. If the learner raises the ceiling instead, the changed workload still exceeds the predeclared policy and the repair has changed requirements rather than correcting the causal omission.
sections.callout: Protecting the host requires separate accelerator, host, storage, queue, and recovery controls. One limit cannot substitute for the others.

sections.title: Issue a capacity and cost decision with expiry
paragraphs: State supported workload slices, tested concurrency, latency and throughput distributions, quality gates, resource reservations and limits, minimum headroom, overload behavior, replica assumptions, startup and recovery time, storage, power or cloud cost assumptions, monitoring thresholds, and excluded cases. Separate measured facts from extrapolation.

Re-benchmark after changing model revision, quantization, runtime, driver, accelerator, host, operating system, container, context policy, batching, template, feature flags, traffic distribution, telemetry, or service objective. Capacity evidence expires when the workload or stack it measured no longer matches production.

Worked decision dated 2026-09-21: the offline calculator accepts the synthetic Scenario B slice of at most 4 concurrent requests and 4,000 maximum tokens because its calculated accelerator allocation is 22 GiB against a 23 GiB admission ceiling. It rejects Scenario C at 5 concurrent requests because the calculated allocation is 24 GiB. Host requirement is 18 GiB against 24 GiB, storage requirement is 54 GiB against 80 GiB, idealized artifact transfer is 8 seconds, restart fixture is 45 seconds, and illustrative per-replica daily cost is USD 57.60.

The decision does not approve a real deployment. Exact model/runtime/accelerator compatibility is UNKNOWN, and the latency, throughput, memory-rate, power, quality, startup, and recovery values are synthetic. A realistic decision excludes all real model families and hardware combinations until an exact-stack quarantine load and representative benchmark replace the unknowns. For Meta Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi, or NVIDIA-related candidates, issue separate evidence rather than transferring this fixture result by family name.

Operational limits for the fixture are a 23 GiB accelerator admission ceiling, 24 GiB host limit with 3 GiB explicitly reserved in the host calculation for recovery, 80 GiB storage ceiling including backup and rollback copies, maximum 4,000 tokens, and maximum concurrency 4 for that token boundary. Controlled overload returns capacity_limit before allocation. Monitoring alarms should precede the declared ceilings; exact warning values are UNKNOWN until noise and measurement error are characterized on a real build.

Cost assumptions are USD 2.40 per replica-hour for 24 hours, yielding USD 57.60 per day before storage, network, taxes, support, idle reserve, or regional adjustments. This is an exercise input, not a price quote. Re-benchmark on any model revision, artifact digest, quantization, tokenizer, template, runtime, backend, driver, compute library, accelerator, host, OS, container, batching policy, context/output policy, feature flag, telemetry, traffic distribution, neighboring workload, quality gate, cost basis, or service-objective change. Review is also due within the module's 60-day cadence.

Rubric: complete evidence retains all four original deliverables. A proficient submission has a field-complete compatibility matrix with documented, measured, inferred, or unknown labels; all three accelerator scenarios plus separate host, storage, rollback, startup, bandwidth, workspace, and cost ledgers; a versioned load profile covering warmup, steady, burst, maximum context, overload, cancellation, restart, and recovery; thresholds declared before results; correct percentile, throughput, rejection, and saturation arithmetic; a passing focused repair without weakening validation or denying safe work; and a dated decision that states limits, costs, exclusions, recovery evidence, and re-benchmark triggers. Missing unknown labels, presenting fixtures as hardware measurements, or deleting host and rollback evidence requires revision.

Causal checkpoint: if the conclusion says deployment approved, compare it with the UNKNOWN compatibility cells. The only supported conclusion is that the deterministic capacity policy behaves as specified. Real approval requires the exact integration measurements that this offline lab intentionally does not perform.

Repository entry: [Open the offline capacity repair lab](/training/self-hosted-model-operations/hardware-runtime-and-capacity-planning/lab/README.md). From the repository root, run `node training/self-hosted-model-operations/hardware-runtime-and-capacity-planning/lab/capacity.mjs training/self-hosted-model-operations/hardware-runtime-and-capacity-planning/lab/fixtures/base.json` and `node training/self-hosted-model-operations/hardware-runtime-and-capacity-planning/lab/test/capacity.test.mjs`.
sections.callout: A capacity decision is versioned evidence with exclusions and expiry, not a permanent approval.

activity.title: Build a measured-paper capacity plan
instructions: Create a synthetic exact-stack compatibility matrix and mark every field as documented, measured, inferred, or unknown.
Estimate model, dynamic cache, workspace, host, storage, and rollback capacity for three context and concurrency scenarios.
Design a versioned load profile with warm-up, steady state, burst, maximum context, overload, cancellation, restart, and recovery cases.
Declare pass thresholds and stop conditions before reviewing synthetic results, then identify the first saturated resource and safe admission policy.
Write a capacity decision with supported slices, limits, headroom, costs, overload behavior, excluded cases, and re-benchmark triggers.

Run the starter CLI on fixtures/base.json and fixtures/changed-overload.json. Record the exact outputs and explain why both are incorrectly admitted by the starter when only the changed workload should be rejected.

Edit only capacity.mjs. Replace the defective zero dynamic-cache assignment with the formula implied by the input. Do not edit validation.mjs, the fixtures, the independent reference, or the tests. Do not hardcode scenario names, fixture totals, or unconditional denial.

Run the immutable test command. Use its causal failures to distinguish a missing per-concurrent-request cache term from a changed limit or deny-all workaround. Then rerun both CLI fixtures and compare the results with the explained answer key in the lab README.

For an independent variation, copy changed-overload.json to a new repository-local workspace, change concurrency to 3 without changing the scenario's other numeric inputs, predict dynamic = 6 GiB and total = 20 GiB, then run the repaired CLI. The expected decision is admit true. Explain why this changed input defeats hardcoded handling of only the supplied scenario names.
evidence: An exact-stack compatibility matrix and calculation sheet with uncertainty labels.
A versioned load profile, metric contract, threshold table, and synthetic saturation results.
A dated capacity decision with resource and admission controls, recovery evidence, costs, exclusions, and expiry triggers.
The repaired capacity.mjs, exact base and changed-workload outputs, passing immutable test output, and the learner-created concurrency-3 variation showing dynamic 6 GiB, total 20 GiB, and admit true.

Welcome to Hardware, Runtime, and Capacity
Planning. This lesson answers a practical

question without pretending that a paper
estimate is a benchmark: what exact

serving build can support which workload,
and under what limits? We will build a

compatibility matrix, estimate
accelerator, host, and storage needs,

measure a representative request profile,
find the first saturation boundary,

protect the host during overload, and
issue a dated capacity decision. The

examples are deterministic offline
fixtures. They do not execute a model,

benchmark an accelerator, contact a cloud
provider, or approve a deployment. By the

end, you will have a reproducible plan
with evidence labels, arithmetic, limits,

exclusions, and triggers for measuring
again.

Start with the whole stack, not the model
name. Record the model architecture,

artifact revision and digest, tensor
format, precision or quantization,

tokenizer, prompt template, maximum tested
context, runtime and version, execution

backend, operating system, CPU

and required extensions. For every cell,

measured, inferred, or unknown. Documented

means a cited source states the exact

exact build produced retained evidence.
Inferred means a calculation or analogy

suggests the value, but has not
established it. Unknown means evidence is

an exact quantization, kernel, device,

driver, or runtime combination to
compatible. Load the exact artifact in

either accept or reject it using measured

Because the real artifact, inference

Checkpoint. The arithmetic fits below a 24
GiB device limit, but the exact quantized

Should those matrix cells be marked

measured, inferred, or unknown, and what

percent errors, 23 GiB accelerator, and 24 GiB host. Burst p95 latency is 780
milliseconds and p95 queue is 90 milliseconds, with 10 requests per second,
so it passes. Maximum context has five requests at 4,000 tokens. Its p95 latency
is 790 milliseconds and throughput is 5 requests per second, passing the separate
4 requests per second boundary. Overload offers 10 requests at concurrency 5.
Correct arithmetic requires 24 GiB, so all 10 are rejected before execution for
capacity_limit. Rejection is 10 divided by 10, or 100 percent. Internal error rate is
not applicable because zero requests were admitted. Cancellation records one client
cancellation, four completions, and zero internal errors. Restart is 45 seconds,
below the 60-second limit. Recovery returns to p95 latency 720 milliseconds
and p95 queue 45 milliseconds, with 10 requests per second, so it passes the
steady thresholds. Checkpoint. The overload row says zero
internal errors. Is that a zero percent rate, or is the rate not applicable?
Explain why, and separately calculate the rejection rate. The internal error rate is not applicable
because the denominator, admitted requests, is zero. Calling it zero percent
hides the absence of an eligible denominator. The controlled rejection rate
is 10 divided by 10, or 100 percent, with reason capacity_limit. That is an
intentional overload policy result, not an internal model error. If warmup was
included in steady p95, restore the declared population and recompute rather
than mixing cold-start behavior into the steady objective. Find saturation by increasing concurrency
and request size gradually until a declared boundary is crossed. Record the
first limiting resource and failure mode. In this fixture, 2 requests at 2,000
tokens require 16 GiB, 4 at 4,000 require 22 GiB, and 5 at 4,000 require 24
GiB. The first boundary is the accelerator admission ceiling, caused
by dynamic per-request cache. This is arithmetic evidence, not an observed
hardware out-of-memory event. The policy admits at most 4 concurrent requests when
each may reach 4,000 tokens. Validate units and token fields, reject over-limit
work before allocation with capacity_limit, and do not automatically
retry a nontransient capacity rejection. Keep a bounded queue outside the
calculator, and preserve the 1 GiB gap between the 23 GiB admission ceiling and a
nominal 24 GiB device class. Separately protect the host. The 24 GiB host limit
includes 3 GiB recovery headroom. Container and scheduler requests or limits
are controls, not proof of application fit. A deny-all repair is also wrong: it
would reject safe Scenario B. Raising the ceiling changes the policy rather than
fixing the missing cache term. Issue a dated decision with scope and
expiry. State supported workload slices, tested concurrency, latency and throughput
distributions, quality gates, resource reservations and limits, headroom,
overload behavior, replica assumptions, startup and recovery, storage, cost
assumptions, monitoring thresholds, and excluded cases. The fixture decision dated
September 21, 2026 supports Scenario B at no more than 4 concurrent requests and
4,000 maximum tokens because calculated accelerator allocation is 22 GiB under the
23 GiB ceiling. It rejects Scenario C at 5 concurrent requests because
allocation is 24 GiB. Host is 18 GiB against 24 GiB. Storage is 54 GiB against
80 GiB. Idealized transfer is 8 seconds, restart is 45 seconds, and
illustrative cost is 57 dollars and 60 cents per replica-day. This is not real
deployment approval. Exact compatibility, latency, throughput, memory rate, power,
quality, startup, and recovery for a real model remain unknown. Re-benchmark after a
model revision, digest, quantization, tokenizer, template, runtime, backend,
driver, library, accelerator, host, operating system, container, batching or
context policy, feature flag, telemetry change, traffic change, neighboring
workload, quality gate, cost basis, or service-objective change. The module also
has a 60-day review cadence. Evidence expires when the measured stack or
workload no longer matches production. Checkpoint. May this deterministic fixture
be written as approval for a real service because Scenario B passes its arithmetic?
State the strongest conclusion that the evidence supports. The supported conclusion is narrower: the
deterministic capacity policy behaves as specified for the synthetic Scenario B
slice, while Scenario C is rejected. It does not approve a real deployment. The
unknown exact compatibility cells require a quarantined integration load, and
synthetic latency, throughput, memory, power, quality, startup, and recovery
values require representative exact-build measurements. A capacity decision is
versioned evidence with exclusions and expiry, not a permanent approval. Now build the measured-paper capacity
plan. Create the exact-stack matrix and label every field. Estimate all three
accelerator scenarios, plus host, storage, rollback, startup, and cost. Design the
versioned load profile with warmup, steady, burst, maximum context, overload,
cancellation, restart, and recovery. Declare thresholds before inspecting
results. Identify accelerator cache as the first fixture boundary, preserve host
recovery headroom, and write supported slices, limits, costs, exclusions,
overload behavior, and re-benchmark triggers. Then repair the offline lab. The
starter has one defect: dynamicGiB is assigned zero. Edit only capacity.mjs and
replace that assignment with concurrency times maximum tokens divided by 1,000,
times cacheGiBPerKTokens. Do not edit validation, fixtures, the independent
reference, or tests. Do not hardcode scenario names, totals, or unconditional
denial. The lab is offline and deterministic. It
has no dependencies, model download, cloud call, credential, container, or charge.
The supplied starter outputs show base-safe with dynamicGiB zero, totalGiB
14, and admit true. The changed-overload starter also shows dynamicGiB zero,
totalGiB 14, and admit true, which is wrong because its cache is omitted. The
starter test reports two passes and two failures. After the one-line formula
repair, the supplied base output has dynamicGiB 8, totalGiB 22, withinLimit
true, and admit true. The supplied changed-overload output has dynamicGiB 10,
totalGiB 24, withinLimit false, and admit false. The immutable test reports four
passes and zero failures. A false result for every input would not be a repair
because it would reject the genuine 22 GiB base case. The validator must also
remain unchanged, so malformed JSON or invalid fields continue to be rejected
rather than being silently accepted. Changed-input task. Copy the
changed-overload fixture into a repository-local workspace. Change only
workload concurrency from 5 to 3. Before running the repaired calculator, predict
the result. Keep maximum tokens at 4,000, base at 14 GiB, cache rate at 0.5 GiB, and
all host and storage inputs unchanged. Write the dynamic cache,
total, within-limit result, and admission decision. Also explain why this changed
valid input defeats a solution hardcoded to the two supplied scenario names. Now compare with the answer. Dynamic cache
is 3 times 4 times 0.5, which equals 6 GiB. Total is 14 plus 6, which
equals 20 GiB. Twenty is below the 23 GiB ceiling, so withinLimit
is true and admit is true, assuming host and storage remain within their
limits. The result must retain the copied scenario string while changing those
calculated values. This changed input defeats hardcoded handling because the
formula responds to concurrency. It also defeats deny-all logic, because this valid
case must be admitted. If the result differs, inspect whether the formula reads
concurrency, maximum tokens, and the cache rate, then preserve validation and the
conjunction of accelerator, host, and storage checks. Begin the knowledge check when you can
explain the complete compatibility stack, why weight memory alone is insufficient,
how a representative profile differs from an unrelated benchmark, how admission and
overload controls protect the host, why controlled rejection is distinct from
internal error, and when capacity must be re-benchmarked. The check contains six
questions. You need at least 80 percent. Choose Begin knowledge check when you are
ready. The activity and check are separate, so you may return to the
worksheet first. Take away four rules. Compatibility is
exact and evidence-labeled. Sizing is a hypothesis that must include dynamic
cache, workspace, host, storage, recovery, and headroom. Capacity comes from a
versioned representative profile with explicit percentile and denominator rules.
Finally, a decision is bounded: it names supported slices, admission behavior,
costs, exclusions, and the changes that require a new benchmark. In this fixture,
22 GiB is admitted, 24 GiB is rejected at a 23 GiB ceiling, and neither
result certifies a real model service. Keep the arithmetic, the unknowns, and the
evidence together.
instructorScript.reducedMotionAlternative: Keep the complete matrix visible. Highlight one row at a time with a text label and no motion. Use a static ledger table with formulas and evidence labels. Do not animate resource bars. Reveal the arithmetic as static lines with no animated counters. Present the entire table without animated charts or gauges. Use a static table and text labels instead of an animated saturation curve. Show the complete decision record as a static form with explicit evidence labels. Keep the four rules on screen without animation.

questions.prompt: What belongs in an exact-stack compatibility record?
choices: Artifact, format, quantization, runtime, backend, OS, device, driver, container, and features
questions.explanation: Compatibility emerges from the complete versioned combination.

questions.prompt: Why is weight memory alone insufficient for sizing?
choices: Dynamic caches, workspace, concurrency, replicas, host services, and headroom also consume resources
questions.explanation: Serving includes material static and dynamic memory beyond the weight bytes.

questions.prompt: Which load profile is most useful?
choices: A versioned representative distribution with cold, warm, burst, boundary, overload, restart, and recovery cases
questions.explanation: Capacity must cover the expected distribution and consequential boundaries.

questions.prompt: What should happen as a service approaches saturation?
choices: Apply declared admission, queue, limit, timeout, shedding, and retry behavior
questions.explanation: Controlled overload prevents resource exhaustion and ambiguous failure.

questions.prompt: What does a published benchmark establish for your endpoint?
choices: Useful external evidence about a stated benchmark setup, not a substitute for exact-build measurement
questions.explanation: Benchmark scope must not be generalized beyond its workload and configuration.

choices: After material stack, model, workload, policy, or service-objective changes
questions.explanation: Capacity evidence is tied to the measured stack and request distribution.
